sections.h2: Where is the Marion County recorder's counter in Ocala?
sections.html:
Official Records sits in the Clerk of Court Annex Building at 19 N Pine Avenue, room 124 on the first floor, in Ocala. Its hours are weekdays, 8:00 am until 5:00 pm, and the desk answers at 352-671-5630.

Mail goes to Clerk of Court and Comptroller, Attn: Recording, P.O. Box 1030, Ocala, FL 34478-1030. Overnight couriers use a different street address, 110 NW 1st Avenue, Ocala, FL 34475. Keeping those two apart saves a missed delivery, since a courier cannot deliver to a post office box.

The Clerk is the county recorder, so one general series of Official Records books holds deeds, mortgages, liens, contracts, affidavits, plats, condominium declarations, bills of sale, judgments, military discharge certificates and declarations of domicile.

sections.h2: Can a Marion County deed be recorded without leaving the office or home?
sections.html:
Yes, through an approved e-recording vendor. The Clerk accepts submissions from CSC eRecording Solutions, eRecording Partners Network and Simplifile, and says it cannot recommend or endorse any of them. A computer, a scanner and internet access are the stated requirements.

The Clerk's page frames the benefits as no check writing, no runner or mailing cost, and keeping the original document in your hands. Documents for e-recording must come through a third-party vendor, so you cannot upload one directly to the Clerk.

sections.h2: How does Marion County's Property Alert service work?
sections.html:
It sends a notice when a document is recorded against a parcel or a name you register. The Clerk calls it the first step in protecting your property, and is direct that it does not prevent fraud. If an alert looks wrong, the owner must contact law enforcement or take legal action.

  • Register a username and password, then confirm through the emailed link.
  • Find the Parcel ID on the Property Appraiser's site by owner name or site address.
  • Register party names in index order, with surname first, such as Smith John A or Smith John Jr.
  • Add several spellings, including middle names and initials, to widen the net.

Use the Official Records Search to see how names appeared on past recordings before you decide what variations to enter.

sections.h2: Which Marion County offices sit beside the Clerk?
sections.html:
Three offices cover most of a property transaction: the Clerk records, the Property Appraiser values, and the Tax Collector bills. Their websites list different tools.

OfficeDetails from its siteUseful tools
Clerk, Official Records19 N Pine Ave, room 124, Ocala; 352-671-5630Search, e-recording, Property Alert
Property Appraiser501 SE 25th Avenue, Ocala; (352) 368-8300Property and sales search, Map It+, homestead e-file, tax estimator, TRIM notice, value adjustment board
Tax Collector(352) 368-8200Pay online, installment plan, deferred taxes, tax deed applications, tourist tax

Sources: Clerk, Property Appraiser, Tax Collector.

The appraiser welcomes walk-ins or appointments, and offers a mortgage estimate letter, a mailing address change request and links for reporting homestead fraud or property damage. The Tax Collector's notice says the 2026 real estate, tangible personal property and railroad rolls are open for collection.

sections.h2: How are Marion County recording charges built?
sections.html:
Recording charges follow the schedule in section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes: a set amount for the first sheet, a smaller amount for each additional sheet, a modest charge for names beyond the fourth, and separate per-sheet trust fund and technology add-ons. Plats and tax deed applications use their own lines. Ask the Official Records desk for a total before sending a check.

Deeds also draw documentary stamp tax under section 201.02, assessed on the consideration, which counts any mortgage tied to the property. All signers are liable regardless of who agrees to pay, and the Clerk gathers it at recording.

sections.h2: Why should a Marion County seller search Official Records first?
sections.html:
The search shows what a buyer's title agent will find. A recorded lien, an old mortgage without a release or a stray affidavit can hold up a closing, and each is easier to fix before a contract.

  • Search your own name in every form you have used.
  • Check the parcel for recorded declarations that bind the lot.
  • Match the legal description on the last deed to the one you plan to sign.
  • Sign deeds before two witnesses, which Florida requires for a conveyance of land.

sections.h2: What else does the Marion County Clerk do besides recording?
sections.html:
The Clerk is one of five constitutional officers elected countywide, and the office's own site lists several roles: county recorder, clerk to the Board of County Commissioners, custodian of county funds and county auditor. As clerk to the commission, the office records and indexes the minutes of Board meetings, which matters if a rezoning or road decision affects a neighborhood.

The same office accepts passport applications as an agent for the U.S. Department of State and forwards them for processing. For property owners, two other services stand out. Petitions to the Value Adjustment Board were opened for e-filing in July 2026, and a searchable database on the site carries information about respondents in injunctions for the protection of a minor, under section 28.2221(8) of the Florida Statutes.

sections.h2: How do Marion County tax deed sales work?
sections.html:
They run online. The Clerk's records page says tax deed sales are open to the public, held through the RealAuction platform, and scheduled once or twice a month on Wednesdays beginning at 9:00 a.m. The Tax Collector's site separately offers an online application for a tax deed and a way to purchase county-held certificates.

For a seller, the timing is the lesson. Unpaid taxes can move a parcel from a bill to a certificate to a public sale, and a recorded tax deed will show up in Official Records. Clear any open balance with the Tax Collector at (352) 368-8200 before it reaches that stage, and keep an eye out for installment or deferral options, which the Tax Collector's menu lists as separate pages.

sections.h2: What can a buyer learn from the Marion Property Appraiser's site?
sections.html:
The appraiser's home page links a property search, a Map It+ tool, a sales search and a property tax estimator, plus an e-file form for homestead exemption and for tangible personal property returns. It also lists a TRIM notice page, the Value Adjustment Board, a code list and a frequently asked questions page with important dates.

  • Use the sales search to see what nearby homes recorded.
  • Use the estimator to test a purchase price, since a sale resets assessed value for most homes.
  • Request a mortgage estimate letter if a lender asks for tax figures.
  • Report suspected homestead fraud through the link on the home page.

faqs.q: Which Marion County desk takes a deed for the record?
faqs.a: At the Clerk's Official Records department, 19 N Pine Avenue, room 124, in Ocala, or through an approved e-recording vendor.

faqs.q: What is the mailing address for Marion County recording?
faqs.a: Clerk of Court and Comptroller, Attn: Recording, P.O. Box 1030, Ocala, FL 34478-1030. Overnight couriers use 110 NW 1st Avenue, Ocala, FL 34475.

faqs.q: Which vendors does Marion County accept for e-recording?
faqs.a: CSC eRecording Solutions, eRecording Partners Network and Simplifile. The Clerk does not endorse any vendor.

faqs.q: Does Property Alert stop property fraud?
faqs.a: No. It tells you when a matching document is recorded. You must contact law enforcement or take legal action if an alert looks unauthorized.

faqs.q: Who values my Marion County home?
faqs.a: The Property Appraiser, at 501 SE 25th Avenue in Ocala, phone (352) 368-8300. The Tax Collector at (352) 368-8200 handles the bill.
